units.en: So the son of Menoetius was attending to the hurt of Eurypylus within the tent, but the Argives and Trojans still fought desperately, nor were the trench and the high wall above it, to keep the Trojans in check longer. They had built it to protect their ships, and had dug the trench all round it that it might safeguard both the ships and the rich spoils which they had taken, but they had not offered hecatombs to the gods. It had been built without the consent of the immortals, and therefore it did not last. So long as Hector lived and Achilles nursed his anger, and so long as the city of Priam remained untaken, the great wall of the Achaeans stood firm; but when the bravest of the Trojans were no more, and many also of the Argives, though some were yet left alive—when, moreover, the city was sacked in the tenth year, and the Argives had gone back with their ships to their own country—then Neptune and Apollo took counsel to destroy the wall, and they turned on to it the streams of all the rivers from Mount Ida into the sea, Rhesus, Heptaporus, Caresus, Rhodius, Grenicus, Aesopus, and goodly Scamander, with Simois, where many a shield and helm had fallen, and many a hero of the race of demigods had bitten the dust. Phoebus Apollo turned the mouths of all these rivers together and made them flow for nine days against the wall, while Jove rained the whole time that he might wash it sooner into the sea. Neptune himself, trident in hand, surveyed the work and threw into the sea all the foundations of beams and stones which the Achaeans had laid with so much toil; he made all level by the mighty stream of the Hellespont, and then when he had swept the wall away he spread a great beach of sand over the place where it had been. This done he turned the rivers back into their old courses.
units.ja: こうしてメノイティオスの子は天幕のなかでエウリュピュロスの傷の手当てにあたっていたが、アルゴス勢とトロイア勢はなおも必死に戦い続けており、堀とその上の高い城壁も、もはや長くトロイア勢を阻むことはできなかった。アカイア勢は船を守るためにこの壁を築き、船と、奪い取った多くの戦利品との双方を守れるように、その周りに堀を掘りめぐらせた。しかし彼らは神々に百牛の犠牲を捧げていなかった。壁は不死の神々の同意なしに築かれたものだったので、長くはもたなかったのである。ヘクトルが生き、アキレウスが怒りを抱き続け、プリアモスの都が攻め落とされずにいるあいだは、アカイア勢の大いなる城壁は揺るがずに立っていた。しかしトロイア勢のうち最も勇敢な者たちが倒れ、アルゴス勢も多くが倒れ——もっとも、なお生き残った者もあった——さらに十年目に都が略奪され、アルゴス勢が船で故国へ帰っていったとき、ポセイドンとアポロンは城壁を壊すことを相談し、イデ山から海へ流れ下るすべての川の流れを壁に向けた。レソス、ヘプタポロス、カレソス、ロディオス、グレニコス、アイソポス、そして美しいスカマンドロスとシモエイス——そこでは多くの盾と兜が落ち、多くの半神の血を引く英雄が土に伏した。ポイボス・アポロンはこれらすべての川の河口を一つに合わせ、九日のあいだ壁に向かって流れさせ、そのあいだゼウスは、壁をより早く海へ洗い流してしまおうとして雨を降らせ続けた。ポセイドン自らは三叉の矛を手に、その業をひととおり見渡し、アカイア勢が苦労して据えた梁や石の土台をことごとく海へ投げ込んだ。彼はヘレスポントスの大きな流れでことごとく平らにし、城壁を洗い去り終えると、そこが壁のあった場所の上に砂の大いなる浜を広げた。そうしてしまってから、彼は川々を元の流路へと戻した。

notes.title: メノイティオスの子
notes.body: アキレウスの親友パトロクロスのこと。ここでは負傷したエウリュピュロスの手当てをしており、戦列を離れている。
notes.bodyEn: This refers to Patroclus, Achilles' close friend. Here he is tending the wounded Eurypylos and is away from the battle line.

units.en: This was what Neptune and Apollo were to do in after time; but as yet battle and turmoil were still raging round the wall till its timbers rang under the blows that rained upon them. The Argives, cowed by the scourge of Jove, were hemmed in at their ships in fear of Hector the mighty minister of Rout, who as heretofore fought with the force and fury of a whirlwind. As a lion or wild boar turns fiercely on the dogs and men that attack him, while these form a solid wall and shower their javelins as they face him—his courage is all undaunted, but his high spirit will be the death of him; many a time does he charge at his pursuers to scatter them, and they fall back as often as he does so—even so did Hector go about among the host exhorting his men, and cheering them on to cross the trench.
units.ja: これこそポセイドンとアポロンが後の世に行うはずのことであった。しかしこのときはまだ、戦いと混乱は城壁の周りで燃えさかっており、浴びせられる打撃に壁の材木が響くほどだった。アルゴス勢はゼウスの鞭に怯え、敗走を司る力強い代行者ヘクトルを恐れて、船のあたりに押し込められていた。ヘクトルはこれまでどおり、つむじ風の力と激しさをもって戦っていた。獅子や野猪が、襲いかかる犬や狩人たちに向かって獰猛に立ち向かうとき——彼らは堅い壁となって並び、対峙しながら投げ槍を雨のように降らせる——その勇気は少しもくじけないが、その誇り高い気概があだとなって我が身の死を招くことになる。彼は何度も追い手に突撃して散らそうとし、そのたびに相手は後ずさる。それと同じように、ヘクトルは軍勢のなかをめぐり、将兵を励まし、堀を渡るよう叱咤した。

notes.title: 「敗走」という語
notes.body: 原文では「敗走（パニック）」は擬人化された戦場の力として語られ、ヘクトルはその「奉仕者・代行者」とされる。敵を恐怖で崩す戦いぶりを表す言い回し。
notes.bodyEn: In the source text, "Rout (Panic)" is spoken of as a personified force of the battlefield, and Hector is called its "servant and agent." It is an expression describing a manner of fighting that breaks the enemy through terror.

units.en: But the horses dared not do so, and stood neighing upon its brink, for the width frightened them. They could neither jump it nor cross it, for it had overhanging banks all round upon either side, above which there were the sharp stakes that the sons of the Achaeans had planted so close and strong as a defence against all who would assail it; a horse, therefore, could not get into it and draw his chariot after him, but those who were on foot kept trying their very utmost. Then Polydamas went up to Hector and said, “Hector, and you other captains of the Trojans and allies, it is madness for us to try and drive our horses across the trench; it will be very hard to cross, for it is full of sharp stakes, and beyond these there is the wall. Our horses therefore cannot get down into it, and would be of no use if they did; moreover it is a narrow place and we should come to harm. If, indeed, great Jove is minded to help the Trojans, and in his anger will utterly destroy the Achaeans, I would myself gladly see them perish now and here far from Argos; but if they should rally and we are driven back from the ships pell-mell into the trench there will be not so much as a man get back to the city to tell the tale. Now, therefore, let us all do as I say; let our squires hold our horses by the trench, but let us follow Hector in a body on foot, clad in full armour, and if the day of their doom is at hand the Achaeans will not be able to withstand us.”
units.ja: しかし馬たちは渡ろうとはせず、堀の縁でいななきながら立ち止まった。堀の幅が彼らを恐れさせたのである。馬はそれを跳び越えることも渡ることもできなかった。堀の両側にはいたるところで岸が張り出し、その上には、アカイア勢の子らが、攻めかかる者すべてに対する防備として、びっしりと頑丈に植えた鋭い杭があった。したがって馬は堀に降りて戦車を引き連れて入ることはできず、歩兵たちだけが必死に試み続けた。そこでポリュダマスがヘクトルのもとへ進み出て言った。「ヘクトル、ならびにトロイア勢と同盟軍の他の将たちよ、われらが馬を駆って堀を越えようとするのは無分別というものです。越えるのはきわめて難しく、堀は鋭い杭で満ち、その向こうには城壁があります。ゆえにわれらの馬は堀に降りることもできず、降りたところで役には立ちますまい。そのうえ狭い場所ですから、われらは損害を受けるでしょう。もし偉大なゼウスがトロイア勢を助けようと思し召し、怒りをもってアカイア勢をことごとく滅ぼそうとなさるのなら、私とて彼らが今ここで、アルゴスから遠く離れて滅びるのを喜んで見ましょう。しかし、もし彼らが持ちこたえ、われらが船から追い立てられて入り乱れて堀へなだれ込むようなことになれば、都へ戻ってそのことを語る者が一人としていなくなるでしょう。だから今は、皆で私の言うとおりにしましょう。従者たちは堀のほとりでわれらの馬を押さえ、われらは鎧を身に着け、徒歩で隊をなしてヘクトルのあとに続こうではありませんか。もし彼らの滅びの日が間近に迫っているのなら、アカイア勢はわれらを防ぎきれないはずです。」

units.en: Thus spoke Polydamas and his saying pleased Hector, who sprang in full armour to the ground, and all the other Trojans, when they saw him do so, also left their chariots. Each man then gave his horses over to his charioteer in charge to hold them ready for him at the trench. Then they formed themselves into companies, made themselves ready, and in five bodies followed their leaders. Those that went with Hector and Polydamas were the bravest and most in number, and the most determined to break through the wall and fight at the ships. Cebriones was also joined with them as third in command, for Hector had left his chariot in charge of a less valiant soldier. The next company was led by Paris, Alcathous, and Agenor; the third by Helenus and Deiphobus, two sons of Priam, and with them was the hero Asius—Asius, the son of Hyrtacus, whose great black horses of the breed that comes from the river Selleis had brought him from Arisbe. Aeneas, the valiant son of Anchises, led the fourth; he and the two sons of Antenor, Archelochus and Acamas, men well versed in all the arts of war. Sarpedon was captain over the allies, and took with him Glaucus and Asteropaeus whom he deemed most valiant after himself—for he was far the best man of them all. These helped to array one another in their ox-hide shields, and then charged straight at the Danaans, for they felt sure that they would not hold out longer and that they should themselves now fall upon the ships.
units.ja: ポリュダマスはこう語り、その言葉はヘクトルを喜ばせた。ヘクトルは鎧を着けたまま地に跳び降り、それを見た他のトロイア勢も皆、戦車を離れた。それぞれが自分の馬を御者に託し、堀のそばでいつでも使えるよう押さえさせた。次に彼らは部隊を編成し、支度を整え、五つの隊となってそれぞれの指揮官に従った。ヘクトルとポリュダマスに従う者たちが最も勇敢で、数も最も多く、城壁を破って船のところまで戦い込もうという決意も最も固かった。ケブリオネスもまた、三人目の指揮官として彼らに加わった。ヘクトルは自分の戦車を、それほど勇敢でない兵に託していたからである。次の隊はパリス、アルカトオス、アゲノルが率いた。第三の隊はプリアモスの二人の子、ヘレノスとデイポボスが率い、そこには勇者アシオスも加わっていた——アシオスはヒュルタコスの子であり、セレエイス河のほとりに発する血統の大きな黒馬たちが、彼をアリュベーから運んできたのである。四番目の隊は、アンキセスの勇敢な子アイネイアスが率いた。彼とともにアンテノルの二人の子、アルケロコスとアカマスがいた。戦いの術に通じた者たちである。同盟軍の総指揮はサルペドンが執り、彼自身の次に最も勇敢と見なすグラウコスとアステロパイオスを伴っていた——なにしろ彼は誰よりもはるかに優れた武将だったのである。彼らは互いに牛革の盾を整えて装い、まっすぐにダナオス勢へと突撃した。アカイア勢がこれ以上持ちこたえられず、今こそ自分たちが船に襲いかかる番だと、固く信じていたからである。

notes.title: サルペドン
notes.body: トロイア側の同盟軍を率いるリュキアの武将・王で、ゼウスの子とされる。この隊列では同盟諸隊の総指揮を執る立場にある。
notes.bodyEn: A Lycian commander and king who leads the allied forces on the Trojan side, said to be a son of Zeus. In this array he holds overall command of the allied contingents.

units.en: The rest of the Trojans and their allies now followed the counsel of Polydamas but Asius, son of Hyrtacus, would not leave his horses and his esquire behind him; in his foolhardiness he took them on with him towards the ships, nor did he fail to come by his end in consequence. Nevermore was he to return to wind-beaten Ilius, exulting in his chariot and his horses; ere he could do so, death of ill-omened name had overshadowed him and he had fallen by the spear of Idomeneus the noble son of Deucalion. He had driven towards the left wing of the ships, by which way the Achaeans used to return with their chariots and horses from the plain. Hither he drove and found the gates with their doors opened wide, and the great bar down—for the gatemen kept them open so as to let those of their comrades enter who might be flying towards the ships. Hither of set purpose did he direct his horses, and his men followed him with a loud cry, for they felt sure that the Achaeans would not hold out longer, and that they should now fall upon the ships. Little did they know that at the gates they should find two of the bravest chieftains, proud sons of the fighting Lapithae—the one, Polypoetes, mighty son of Pirithous, and the other Leonteus, peer of murderous Mars. These stood before the gates like two high oak trees upon the mountains, that tower from their wide-spreading roots, and year after year battle with wind and rain—even so did these two men await the onset of great Asius confidently and without flinching. The Trojans led by him and by Iamenus, Orestes, Adamas the son of Asius, Thoon and Oenomaus, raised a loud cry of battle and made straight for the wall, holding their shields of dry ox-hide above their heads; for a while the two defenders remained inside and cheered the Achaeans on to stand firm in the defence of their ships; when, however, they saw that the Trojans were attacking the wall, while the Danaans were crying out for help and being routed, they rushed outside and fought in front of the gates like two wild boars upon the mountains that abide the attack of men and dogs, and charging on either side break down the wood all round them tearing it up by the roots, and one can hear the clattering of their tusks, till some one hits them and makes an end of them—even so did the gleaming bronze rattle about their breasts, as the weapons fell upon them; for they fought with great fury, trusting to their own prowess and to those who were on the wall above them. These threw great stones at their assailants in defence of themselves their tents and their ships. The stones fell thick as the flakes of snow which some fierce blast drives from the dark clouds and showers down in sheets upon the earth—even so fell the weapons from the hands alike of Trojans and Achaeans. Helmet and shield rang out as the great stones rained upon them, and Asius, the son of Hyrtacus, in his dismay cried aloud and smote his two thighs. “Father Jove,” he cried, “of a truth you too are altogether given to lying. I made sure the Argive heroes could not withstand us, whereas like slim-waisted wasps, or bees that have their nests in the rocks by the wayside—they leave not the holes wherein they have built undefended, but fight for their little ones against all who would take them—even so these men, though they be but two, will not be driven from the gates, but stand firm either to slay or be slain.”
units.ja: 残りのトロイア勢とその同盟軍は、こんどはポリュダマスの進言に従ったが、ヒュルタコスの子アシオスだけは、自分の馬と従者を後に残そうとしなかった。無謀にも彼らを連れて船の方へと進み、そのために最期を迎えることになった。彼が風に打たれるイリオスへ、戦車と馬に意気揚々と帰ることは二度となかった。そうする間もなく、忌まわしい名の死が彼をおおい、高貴なデウカリオンの子イードメネウスの槍に倒れたのである。彼は船団の左翼の方へと戦車を駆っていた。そこは、アカイア勢が戦車と馬を連れて平原から戻ってくるのに通っていた道であった。そこへ彼は駆けつけ、門扉が大きく開かれ、大きな横木が下ろされているのを見た。門番たちは、船の方へ逃れてくる味方を通すために、門を開けたままにしていたのである。彼はわざとこの方へ馬を向け、部下たちは大声をあげて従った。アカイア勢はもう持ちこたえられまい、今こそ船に襲いかかれると確信していたからである。彼らは知る由もなかった。門のところで、最も勇敢な二人の武将——勇猛なラピテス族の誇り高き子ら——に出会うことになろうとは。一人はペイリトオスの強き子ポリュポイテス、もう一人は人殺しのアレスにも比すべきレオンテウスである。この二人は門の前に、山にそびえる二本の高い樫の木のように立っていた。その木は広く張った根からそびえ立ち、年ごとに風と雨と戦っている——ちょうどそのように、この二人も、大いなるアシオスの攻撃を確信をもって、ひるむことなく待ち受けた。彼と、イアメノス、オレステス、アシオスの子アダマス、トオーン、オイノマオスに率いられたトロイア勢は、戦いの鬨の声をあげ、乾いた牛皮の盾を頭上に掲げて、まっすぐ塀へと向かった。しばらくの間、守る二人は内側にとどまって、アカイア勢に船を守って踏みとどまるよう励ましていた。しかし、トロイア勢が塀を攻め、ダナオス勢が助けを叫びながら崩れていくのを見ると、二人は外へ飛び出し、山にいる二頭の野猪のように門の前で戦った。その猪は人と犬の攻撃をじっと受け止め、左右に突進して周りの森を押し倒し、根こそぎ引き抜き、牙のぶつかる音が聞こえるほどだが、ついに誰かに撃たれて命を終える——ちょうどそのように、武器が打ちつけられるたび、輝く青銅が二人の胸のあたりで鳴り響いた。彼らは自分の武勇と、頭上で塀の上に立つ味方とを頼りに、激しい怒りをもって戦っていたのである。塀の上の者たちは、自分たちと天幕と船を守るため、攻め寄せる敵に大きな石を投げつけた。石は、激しい風が暗い雲から雪片を吹き払い、幾重にも地の上に降りしきらせるかのように、密に降り注いだ——ちょうどそのように、トロイア勢とアカイア勢の双方の手から武器が降りそそいだ。大きな石が雨のように降りかかる中で、兜と盾が鳴り響き、ヒュルタコスの子アシオスは、意気消沈して大声をあげ、自分の両腿を打ち叩いた。「父ゼウスよ」と彼は叫んだ。「まことに、あなたも嘘ばかりおっしゃる。アルゴス勢の勇士たちは我らに抗しきれまいと、私は確信していた。ところが彼らは、道端の岩に巣を作る細腰の蜂や蜜蜂のようではないか。蜂は自分が作った穴を守らずに放っておくことはせず、わが子のために、奪おうとする者すべてと戦う——ちょうどそのように、この者たちはたった二人でありながら、門から追い払われることを拒み、殺すか殺されるか、どちらかになるまで踏みとどまっているのだ」。

notes.title: ラピテス族
notes.body: ペイリトオスを王とするテッサリアの伝説的な部族で、ケンタウロスとの戦いで名高い。ホメロスはポリュポイテスとレオンテウスを「槍にすぐれたラピテス族の子ら」として、とりわけ勇敢な守り手に描いている。
notes.bodyEn: A legendary Thessalian tribe whose king was Peirithoos, famous for its battle with the Centaurs. Homer depicts Polypoites and Leonteus as "sons of the spear-skilled Lapiths" and as especially valiant defenders.

units.en: He spoke, but moved not the mind of Jove, whose counsel it then was to give glory to Hector. Meanwhile the rest of the Trojans were fighting about the other gates; I, however, am no god to be able to tell about all these things, for the battle raged everywhere about the stone wall as it were a fiery furnace. The Argives, discomfited though they were, were forced to defend their ships, and all the gods who were defending the Achaeans were vexed in spirit; but the Lapithae kept on fighting with might and main.
units.ja: 彼はこう言ったが、ゼウスの心を動かすことはできなかった。そのときゼウスの計らいは、ヘクトルに栄光を与えることにあったからである。その間、残りのトロイア勢は他の門のあたりで戦っていた。だが、私は神ではないので、これらすべてのことを語ることはできない。石の塀の周りのいたるところで、戦いは燃える炉のように激しく燃えさかっていたからである。アルゴス勢は打ち破られながらも、否応なく自分たちの船を守らねばならなかった。アカイア勢を援ける神々はみな心を痛めていたが、ラピテス族の二人は力を尽くして戦い続けた。

notes.title: 語り手の介入
notes.body: 「私は神ではないので」という一句は、語り手が自らの限界を認め、戦場のすべてを語りきることはできないと断る挿入。この叙事詩の語りが全知ではないことを示す。
notes.bodyEn: The phrase "for I am no god" is an insertion in which the narrator acknowledges his own limits and declares that he cannot tell the whole of the battlefield. It shows that this epic's narration is not omniscient.

units.en: Thereon Polypoetes, mighty son of Pirithous, hit Damasus with a spear upon his cheek-pierced helmet. The helmet did not protect him, for the point of the spear went through it, and broke the bone, so that the brain inside was scattered about, and he died fighting. He then slew Pylon and Ormenus. Leonteus, of the race of Mars, killed Hippomachus the son of Antimachus by striking him with his spear upon the girdle. He then drew his sword and sprang first upon Antiphates whom he killed in combat, and who fell face upwards on the earth. After him he killed Menon, Iamenus, and Orestes, and laid them low one after the other.
units.ja: そこで、ペイリトオスの強き子ポリュポイテスは、ダマソスの頬当てのある兜に槍を突き当てた。兜は彼を守らなかった。槍の穂先は兜を貫き、骨を砕いたので、中の脳は飛び散り、彼は戦いながら死んだ。続いて彼はピュロンとオルメノスを討ち取った。アレスの血を引くレオンテウスは、アンティマコスの子ヒッポマコスを、腰帯のところに槍を突き立てて殺した。次いで彼は剣を抜き、まずアンティパテスに飛びかかって戦いの中で殺した。相手は仰向けに地に倒れた。そのあと彼はメノン、イアメノス、オレステスを殺し、次々に打ち倒した。

notes.title: 討ち取りの列挙
notes.body: 相手の名を次々に挙げて倒していく叙述は、叙事詩に繰り返し現れる定型の戦闘場面。一人ひとりの最期は短く語られ、戦いの密度を伝える。
notes.bodyEn: The narration that names opponents one after another and cuts them down is a formulaic battle scene recurring throughout the epic. Each man's end is told briefly, conveying the density of the fighting.

units.en: While they were busy stripping the armour from these heroes, the youths who were led on by Polydamas and Hector (and these were the greater part and the most valiant of those that were trying to break through the wall and fire the ships) were still standing by the trench, uncertain what they should do; for they had seen a sign from heaven when they had essayed to cross it—a soaring eagle that flew skirting the left wing of their host, with a monstrous blood-red snake in its talons still alive and struggling to escape. The snake was still bent on revenge, wriggling and twisting itself backwards till it struck the bird that held it, on the neck and breast; whereon the bird being in pain, let it fall, dropping it into the middle of the host, and then flew down the wind with a sharp cry. The Trojans were struck with terror when they saw the snake, portent of aegis-bearing Jove, writhing in the midst of them, and Polydamas went up to Hector and said, “Hector, at our councils of war you are ever given to rebuke me, even when I speak wisely, as though it were not well, forsooth, that one of the people should cross your will either in the field or at the council board; you would have them support you always: nevertheless I will say what I think will be best; let us not now go on to fight the Danaans at their ships, for I know what will happen if this soaring eagle which skirted the left wing of our host with a monstrous blood-red snake in its talons (the snake being still alive) was really sent as an omen to the Trojans on their essaying to cross the trench. The eagle let go her hold; she did not succeed in taking it home to her little ones, and so will it be—with ourselves; even though by a mighty effort we break through the gates and wall of the Achaeans, and they give way before us, still we shall not return in good order by the way we came, but shall leave many a man behind us whom the Achaeans will do to death in defence of their ships. Thus would any seer who was expert in these matters, and was trusted by the people, read the portent.”
units.ja: 二人がこれらの勇士から武具を剥ぎ取るのに忙しくしている間、ポリュダマスとヘクトルに率いられた若者たち——塀を破り船に火をかけようとしていた者のうち、大半を占め、最も勇敢な者たちであった——は、どうすべきか迷いながら、なお壕のそばに立ち止まっていた。壕を越えようとしたとき、彼らは天からの徴を見たからである。高く舞い上がる鷲が、自分たちの軍の左翼に沿って飛び、その爪には、血のように赤い巨大な蛇が、まだ生きて逃れようともがきながら掴まれていた。蛇はなおも復讐の心を捨てず、身をくねらせ、逆にのけぞって、自分を掴む鳥の首と胸を打った。鳥は痛みに耐えかねて蛇を放し、軍の真ん中に落とすと、鋭い声をあげて風に乗って飛び去った。アイギスを持つゼウスの徴である蛇が自分たちの中でのたうち回るのを見て、トロイア勢は恐怖に襲われた。ポリュダマスはヘクトルのところへ進み出て言った。「ヘクトルよ、あなたは戦の評定のたびに、私が正しいことを言ってもいつも私を叱責なさる。民の一人が、戦場であれ評定の席であれ、あなたの意志に逆らうのはよくないことだとでもいうように。あなたは皆がいつも自分を支持することをお望みだ。それでも私は、これが最善と思うことを申し上げよう。今はダナオス勢の船のところまで攻めかかって戦うのはやめにしよう。もし、軍の左翼に沿って飛び、爪に血のように赤い巨大な蛇（まだ生きていた）を掴んでいたあの舞い上がる鷲が、まことに、壕を越えようとしたトロイア勢への前兆として遣わされたものなら、何が起こるか私にはわかるのだ。鷲は獲物を手放した。雛のもとへ持ち帰ることはできなかった。我々も同じことになるだろう。たとえ大いなる力をもってアカイア勢の門と塀を破り、彼らが我々の前から退いたとしても、我々は来た道を整然と引き返すことはできず、多くの者を後に残すことになる。アカイア勢は船を守るためにその者たちを殺すだろう。この道に通じ、民に信頼される占い師なら、この前兆をそう読み解くはずだ」。

notes.title: 鳥占い（オイオノス）
notes.body: 飛ぶ鳥の進路、とりわけ左右どちらへ飛ぶかを見て吉凶を占う習慣。獲物を雛のもとへ持ち帰れなかった鷲は、企てを成し遂げられない兆しとして読まれている。
notes.bodyEn: The practice of divining fortune or misfortune by observing the course of birds in flight, especially which way, left or right, they fly. The eagle that failed to carry its prey back to its nestlings is read as a sign of failing to accomplish the undertaking.

units.en: Hector looked fiercely at him and said, “Polydamas, I like not of your reading. You can find a better saying than this if you will. If, however, you have spoken in good earnest, then indeed has heaven robbed you of your reason. You would have me pay no heed to the counsels of Jove, nor to the promises he made me—and he bowed his head in confirmation; you bid me be ruled rather by the flight of wild-fowl. What care I whether they fly towards dawn or dark, and whether they be on my right hand or on my left? Let us put our trust rather in the counsel of great Jove, king of mortals and immortals. There is one omen, and one only—that a man should fight for his country. Why are you so fearful? Though we be all of us slain at the ships of the Argives you are not likely to be killed yourself, for you are not steadfast nor courageous. If you will not fight, or would talk others over from doing so, you shall fall forthwith before my spear.”
units.ja: ヘクトルは鋭く彼を睨んで言った。「ポリュダマス、私はお前の読み方が気に入らぬ。気があれば、もっとましな言葉を見つけられるだろうに。しかし、もし本気でそう言ったのなら、天はお前から正気を奪ってしまったのだ。お前は、ゼウスの計らいにも、彼が私に与えた約束——彼はそれを確証して頭を頷かせた——にも、耳を貸すなと言う。そして、野鳥の飛び方に従えと命じるのだな。鳥が暁の方へ飛ぼうと闇の方へ飛ぼうと、私の右手に来ようと左手に来ようと、私にとって何の関わりがあろうか。むしろ、死すべき者と不死なる者の王である大いなるゼウスの計らいをこそ、我々は信じよう。吉兆はただ一つ、人が自分の国のために戦うこと、それだけだ。なぜそんなに怯えるのか。たとえ我々が皆、アルゴス勢の船のところで討たれたとしても、お前だけは殺されそうにない。お前は堅固でも勇敢でもないからだ。戦おうとせず、あるいは他の者たちを言いくるめて戦わせまいとするなら、お前はただちに私の槍の前に倒れることになるぞ」。

notes.title: 唯一の吉兆
notes.body: ヘクトルは鳥占いを退け、「人が自分の国のために戦うこと」こそ唯一の吉兆だと主張する。人間の勇気と務めを占いより重んじる言葉として後世まで引用される。
notes.bodyEn: Hector rejects bird divination and asserts that "a man fighting for his own country" is the only good omen. The words are quoted down through later ages as valuing human courage and duty above divination.

units.en: With these words he led the way, and the others followed after with a cry that rent the air. Then Jove the lord of thunder sent the blast of a mighty wind from the mountains of Ida, that bore the dust down towards the ships; he thus lulled the Achaeans into security, and gave victory to Hector and to the Trojans, who, trusting to their own might and to the signs he had shown them, essayed to break through the great wall of the Achaeans. They tore down the breastworks from the walls, and overthrew the battlements; they upheaved the buttresses, which the Achaeans had set in front of the wall in order to support it; when they had pulled these down they made sure of breaking through the wall, but the Danaans still showed no sign of giving ground; they still fenced the battlements with their shields of ox-hide, and hurled their missiles down upon the foe as soon as any came below the wall.
units.ja: こう言って彼は先に立って進み、ほかの者たちもそれに続いた。その叫び声は大気を裂くようだった。そこで雷の主ゼウスはイデの山々から強烈な風の一撃を送り、その風は塵を船の方へ吹き下ろした。ゼウスはこうしてアカイア勢を油断させ、ヘクトルとトロイア勢に勝利を与えた。彼らは自らの力を、そしてゼウスが示したしるしを信じて、アカイア勢の大いなる城壁を打ち破ろうと試みた。彼らは城壁から胸塁を引きはがし、狭間壁を打ち倒し、アカイア勢が城壁を支えるためにその前方に立てておいた控え壁を押し起こした。これらを引き倒したとき、彼らは城壁を破れると確信したが、ダナオス勢は依然として退く気配をまったく見せなかった。彼らは今も牛革の盾で狭間壁を防ぎ、敵が城壁の下へやって来るやいなや、その上から投げ槍を浴びせかけた。

notes.title: イデの山々
notes.body: トロイアの南東にそびえる山脈。ゼウスが戦いを見下ろす場所として『イリアス』にたびたび登場する。
notes.bodyEn: A mountain range rising to the southeast of Troy. It appears repeatedly in the Iliad as the place from which Zeus looks down upon the battle.

units.en: The two Ajaxes went about everywhere on the walls cheering on the Achaeans, giving fair words to some while they spoke sharply to any one whom they saw to be remiss. “My friends,” they cried, “Argives one and all—good bad and indifferent, for there was never fight yet, in which all were of equal prowess—there is now work enough, as you very well know, for all of you. See that you none of you turn in flight towards the ships, daunted by the shouting of the foe, but press forward and keep one another in heart, if it may so be that Olympian Jove the lord of lightning will vouchsafe us to repel our foes, and drive them back towards the city.”
units.ja: 二人のアイアスは城壁の上を至るところ巡り歩いてアカイア勢を励まし、ある者には穏やかな言葉をかけ、手を抜いていると見た者には鋭く言った。「友よ」と彼らは叫んだ。「アルゴス勢の者たちよ、一人残らず——すぐれた者も、劣った者も、どっちつかずの者も。というのも、皆が等しく同じ武勇を持つ戦いなど、これまで一度もなかったからだ——今や、皆がよく分かっているとおり、お前たち全員が果たすべき働きがある。敵の叫びに怯えて船の方へ逃げ出す者が一人もいないようにせよ。むしろ前へ進み、互いに勇気を保て。もしかすると、稲妻の主オリュンポスのゼウスが、われらに敵を撃退し、彼らを町の方へ追い返すことをお許しになるかもしれぬ。」

notes.title: アカイア勢・アルゴス勢・ダナオス勢
notes.body: ホメロスは同じギリシア側の軍を、集団の呼び名を変えながら指す。アルゴス勢は中心地アルゴスの名に、ダナオス勢は伝説上の祖ダナオスに由来する。
notes.bodyEn: Homer refers to the same Greek host by varying the name of the group. "Argives" derives from the name of the central city Argos, and "Danaans" from the legendary ancestor Danaus.

units.en: Thus did the two go about shouting and cheering the Achaeans on. As the flakes that fall thick upon a winter’s day, when Jove is minded to snow and to display these his arrows to mankind—he lulls the wind to rest, and snows hour after hour till he has buried the tops of the high mountains, the headlands that jut into the sea, the grassy plains, and the tilled fields of men; the snow lies deep upon the forelands, and havens of the grey sea, but the waves as they come rolling in stay it that it can come no further, though all else is wrapped as with a mantle, so heavy are the heavens with snow—even thus thickly did the stones fall on one side and on the other, some thrown at the Trojans, and some by the Trojans at the Achaeans; and the whole wall was in an uproar.
units.ja: こうして二人は巡り歩き、叫んでアカイア勢を励ました。冬の日に厚く降り積もる雪の吹雪のように——ゼウスが雪を降らせようと思い、この矢を人類に示そうとされるとき、彼は風を静め、何時間も何時間も雪を降らせ続け、高い山々の頂き、海へ突き出た岬、草の茂る平野、人の耕す畑を埋め尽くしてしまう。雪は前山や灰色の海の入り江に深く積もるが、押し寄せる波はそれを遮って、それ以上進ませない。それでもほかのすべてが外套をまとったように覆われるほど、天は雪に重く沈んでいる——それと同じように、石はあちらからもこちらからも密に降り注ぎ、あるものはトロイア勢へ投げられ、あるものはトロイア勢がアカイア勢へと投げた。城壁の全体が轟きに包まれた。

notes.title: 「この矢」＝雪
notes.body: ここでゼウスの「矢」と呼ばれているのは雪のこと。稲妻や雹を矢にたとえる言い方はホメロスに繰り返し見られ、降雪もその一例として描かれている。
notes.bodyEn: What is called Zeus's "arrows" here is snow. The idiom of likening lightning and hail to arrows appears repeatedly in Homer, and snowfall is depicted as one instance of it.

units.en: Still the Trojans and brave Hector would not yet have broken down the gates and the great bar, had not Jove turned his son Sarpedon against the Argives as a lion against a herd of horned cattle. Before him he held his shield of hammered bronze, that the smith had beaten so fair and round, and had lined with ox-hides which he had made fast with rivets of gold all round the shield; this he held in front of him, and brandishing his two spears came on like some lion of the wilderness, who has been long famished for want of meat and will dare break even into a well-fenced homestead to try and get at the sheep. He may find the shepherds keeping watch over their flocks with dogs and spears, but he is in no mind to be driven from the fold till he has had a try for it; he will either spring on a sheep and carry it off, or be hit by a spear from some strong hand—even so was Sarpedon fain to attack the wall and break down its battlements. Then he said to Glaucus son of Hippolochus, “Glaucus, why in Lycia do we receive especial honour as regards our place at table? Why are the choicest portions served us and our cups kept brimming, and why do men look up to us as though we were gods? Moreover we hold a large estate by the banks of the river Xanthus, fair with orchard lawns and wheat-growing land; it becomes us, therefore, to take our stand at the head of all the Lycians and bear the brunt of the fight, that one may say to another, ‘Our princes in Lycia eat the fat of the land and drink best of wine, but they are fine fellows; they fight well and are ever at the front in battle.’ My good friend, if, when we were once out of this fight, we could escape old age and death thenceforward and forever, I should neither press forward myself nor bid you do so, but death in ten thousand shapes hangs ever over our heads, and no man can elude him; therefore let us go forward and either win glory for ourselves, or yield it to another.”
units.ja: それでもトロイア勢と勇敢なヘクトルは、まだ門と大きな横木を打ち壊してはいなかっただろう。もしゼウスが、その子サルペドンを、角ある牛の群れに向かう獅子のようにアルゴス勢へと向けなかったならば。サルペドンは、鍛冶が美しく丸く打ち出し、金の鋲で一面に留めた牛革を裏に張り付けた、鍛造青銅の盾を前に構え、二本の槍を振り回しながら進んだ。ちょうど、肉に長く飢え、羊を狙おうとしっかり囲われた牧場にさえ踏み込もうとする荒野の獅子のように。彼は羊飼いたちが犬と槍で群れを見張っているのを見つけるかもしれないが、一度は試してみるまでは囲いから追い立てられるつもりはない。羊に飛びかかって奪い去るか、さもなくば強い手から投げられた槍に打たれるか、である——ちょうどそのようにサルペドンは、城壁を攻めてその狭間壁を打ち破りたいと願った。そして彼はヒッポロコスの子グラウコスに言った。「グラウコスよ、なぜリュキアでは、われらは食卓の席について格別の名誉を受けるのか。なぜ最上の肉がわれらに供され、杯は常に満たされ、人々はわれらを神々のように仰ぎ見るのか。さらにわれらはクサントス川の岸辺に広大な所領を持ち、果樹園の草地と小麦の実る土地に恵まれている。それゆえわれらは、リュキア人すべての先頭に立って戦いの衝撃を受け止めるべきなのだ。人が互いに『リュキアのわれらの君たちは地の肥えたところを食らい、最上の酒を飲むが、しかし彼らは立派な男たちだ。よく戦い、いつも戦いの最前線にいる』と言えるように。親しい友よ、もしわれらがこの戦いから一度抜け出て、その後は永遠に老いと死から逃れられるのなら、私は自分から前へ進みもせず、お前にもそう勧めないだろう。しかし死は一万の姿をとって常にわれらの頭上に垂れ込めており、誰もそれを逃れることはできない。だからわれらは前へ進み、自ら栄光を勝ち取るか、さもなくばそれを他の者に譲るのだ。」

notes.title: サルペドン
notes.body: ゼウスの子で、南のリュキア勢を率いてトロイア側に加勢する武将。この段落の「獅子」の比喩と、名誉と死をめぐるグラウコスへの言葉が、彼の登場場面として知られる。
notes.bodyEn: A son of Zeus and a commander who leads the Lycian force from the south to aid the Trojan side. The lion simile in this paragraph and his words to Glaucus about honor and death are known as his entrance scene.

units.en: Glaucus heeded his saying, and the pair forthwith led on the host of Lycians. Menestheus son of Peteos was dismayed when he saw them, for it was against his part of the wall that they came—bringing destruction with them; he looked along the wall for some chieftain to support his comrades and saw the two Ajaxes, men ever eager for the fray, and Teucer, who had just come from his tent, standing near them; but he could not make his voice heard by shouting to them, so great an uproar was there from crashing shields and helmets and the battering of gates with a din which reached the skies. For all the gates had been closed, and the Trojans were hammering at them to try and break their way through them. Menestheus, therefore, sent Thootes with a message to Ajax. “Run, good Thootes,” he said, “and call Ajax, or better still bid both come, for it will be all over with us here directly; the leaders of the Lycians are upon us, men who have ever fought desperately heretofore. But if they have too much on their hands to let them come, at any rate let Ajax son of Telamon do so, and let Teucer, the famous bowman, come with him.”
units.ja: グラウコスはその言葉に耳を貸し、二人はただちにリュキアの軍勢を率いて進んだ。ペテオスの子メネステウスは、彼らを見て怯んだ。というのも、彼らは破滅を伴って彼の受け持つ城壁の部分へやって来たからである。彼は仲間を支えてくれる武将はいないかと城壁沿いを見渡し、戦いを常に切望する二人のアイアスと、ちょうど天幕から出てきたばかりのテウクロスが彼らのそばに立っているのを見た。しかし叫んでも彼らに声を届かせることはできなかった。盾と兜のぶつかる音、門を打ち破ろうとする音が、天にまで届く大騒音を立てていたからである。というのも、すべての門は閉ざされており、トロイア勢はそこを打ち破って突破しようと槌を打ちつけていたからである。そこでメネステウスはトオテスをアイアスのもとへ使者として送った。「走れ、良きトオテス」と彼は言った。「アイアスを呼べ。いや、むしろ二人とも来るよう伝えよ。ここはもうすぐ終わりになるだろう。リュキアの将たちがわれらに攻めかかっているのだ、これまでも常に死に物狂いに戦ってきた者たちが。しかしもし彼らが手一杯で来られないなら、せめてテラモンの子アイアスだけでも来させ、名高い弓の名手テウクロスも一緒に来させよ。」

notes.title: メネステウス
notes.body: ペテオスの子で、アテナイ勢の将。作中では目立たない武将だが、この場面では自分の守る城壁区画に危機が迫り、救援を求めて使者を送る。
notes.bodyEn: Son of Peteos and commander of the Athenian force. He is an inconspicuous warrior in the work, but in this scene, with danger closing on the stretch of wall he defends, he sends a messenger to ask for help.

units.en: The messenger did as he was told, and set off running along the wall of the Achaeans. When he reached the Ajaxes he said to them, “Sirs, princes of the Argives, the son of noble Peteos bids you come to him for a while and help him. You had better both come if you can, or it will be all over with him directly; the leaders of the Lycians are upon him, men who have ever fought desperately heretofore; if you have too much on your hands to let both come, at any rate let Ajax, son of Telamon, do so, and let Teucer, the famous bowman, come with him.”
units.ja: 使者は言われたとおりにし、アカイア勢の城壁沿いを走り出した。彼は二人のアイアスのもとに着くと、彼らに言った。「ご両人、アルゴス勢の君たちよ、高貴なペテオスの子がしばらくの間あなた方のもとへ来て彼を助けるよう求めています。もし来られるなら二人とも来た方がよい、さもなくば彼はすぐに終わりになるでしょう。リュキアの将たちが彼に攻めかかっているのです、これまでも常に死に物狂いに戦ってきた者たちが。もしお二人とも来るには手一杯なら、せめてテラモンの子アイアスだけでも来て、名高い弓の名手テウクロスも一緒に来てください。」

units.en: Great Ajax son of Telamon heeded the message, and at once spoke to the son of Oileus. “Ajax,” said he, “do you two, yourself and brave Lycomedes, stay here and keep the Danaans in heart to fight their hardest. I will go over yonder, and bear my part in the fray, but I will come back here at once as soon as I have given them the help they need.”
units.ja: テラモンの子大アイアスはその伝言に耳を貸し、ただちにオイレウスの子に言った。「アイアスよ、お前と勇敢なリュコメデスはここに残り、ダナオス勢の心を保って全力で戦わせよ。私はあちらへ行って戦いの分を果たすが、彼らに必要な助けを与えたらすぐにここへ戻ってくる。」

units.en: With this, Ajax son of Telamon set off, and Teucer, his brother by the same father, went also, with Pandion to carry Teucer’s bow. They went along inside the wall, and when they came to the tower where Menestheus was (and hard pressed indeed did they find him) the brave captains and leaders of the Lycians were storming the battlements as it were a thick dark cloud, fighting in close quarters, and raising the battle-cry aloud.
units.ja: こう言って、テラモンの子アイアスは出発し、同じ父を持つ彼の兄弟テウクロスも、テウクロスの弓を運ぶパンディオンを伴ってともに行った。彼らは城壁の内側を進み、メネステウスのいる櫓に着いたとき——そして実際、彼が苦戦していることよ——リュキアの勇敢な将たちと指導者たちは、厚い暗い雲のように狭間壁を襲い、近接戦を戦い、高声でときの声を上げていた。

notes.title: テウクロス
notes.body: テラモンの子で大アイアスの兄弟（同じ父、別の母）。トロイア戦でギリシア側随一の弓の名手として描かれ、この場面でも弓を携えて救援に加わる。
notes.bodyEn: Son of Telamon and brother of Great Ajax (same father, different mother). He is depicted as the foremost archer on the Greek side in the Trojan War, and in this scene too he joins the relief with his bow.

units.en: First, Ajax son of Telamon killed brave Epicles, a comrade of Sarpedon, hitting him with a jagged stone that lay by the battlements at the very top of the wall. As men now are, even one who is in the bloom of youth could hardly lift it with his two hands, but Ajax raised it high aloft and flung it down, smashing Epicles’ four-crested helmet so that the bones of his head were crushed to pieces, and he fell from the high wall as though he were diving, with no more life left in him. Then Teucer wounded Glaucus the brave son of Hippolochus as he was coming on to attack the wall. He saw his shoulder bare and aimed an arrow at it, which made Glaucus leave off fighting. Thereon he sprang covertly down for fear some of the Achaeans might see that he was wounded and taunt him. Sarpedon was stung with grief when he saw Glaucus leave him, still he did not leave off fighting, but aimed his spear at Alcmaon the son of Thestor and hit him. He drew his spear back again and Alcmaon came down headlong after it with his bronzed armour rattling round him. Then Sarpedon seized the battlement in his strong hands, and tugged at it till it all gave way together, and a breach was made through which many might pass.
units.ja: まずテラモンの子アイアスが、サルペドンの僚友である勇敢なエピクレスを討った。城壁のいちばん上の胸壁のかたわらにあった、ぎざぎざの石を投げ当てたのである。今の人間であれば、若さの盛りの者でも両手でようやく持ち上げられるかどうかというその石を、アイアスは高く差し上げて投げおろし、エピクレスの四つの飾り房のある兜を打ち砕いて、頭の骨を粉々にしてしまった。エピクレスは高い城壁から、まるで飛び込むかのように落ちて、息絶えた。次にテウクロスが、城壁を攻めようと進んでいた、ヒッポロコスの子の勇敢なグラウコスを射て傷つけた。彼はグラウコスの肩がむき出しになっているのを見て、そこに矢を狙い当てた。グラウコスは戦いをやめざるを得なくなった。そこで彼は、アカイア勢に傷ついているところを見られて嘲られるのを恐れ、人目を忍んで飛び降りた。サルペドンは、グラウコスが自分から離れるのを見て悲しみに胸を刺されたが、それでも戦いをやめず、テストルの子アルクマオンに槍を狙い当てて突き刺した。彼が槍を引き抜くと、アルクマオンはその後を追うように真っ逆さまに落ち、その周りで青銅の鎧が鳴り響いた。そこでサルペドンは強い両手で胸壁をつかみ、みな一緒に崩れ落ちるまで引き揺すった。多くの者が通れるだけの缺口が開いた。

notes.title: 「今の人間なら」の定型句
notes.body: ホメロス叙事詩には、英雄が持ち上げる石の重さを「今の人間では若者二人がかりでも」と述べて、その怪力と遠い昔の英雄時代を際立たせる言い回しが繰り返し現れる。ここではアイアスの力が強調されている。
notes.titleEn: The Formula "Such as Men Now Are"
notes.bodyEn: In Homer's epics there recurs an expression that states the weight of the stone a hero lifts could not be moved "by two men such as men now are, even as young men," setting off his prodigious strength and the far-off age of heroes. Here Ajax's strength is emphasized.

units.en: Ajax and Teucer then both of them attacked him. Teucer hit him with an arrow on the band that bore the shield which covered his body, but Jove saved his son from destruction that he might not fall by the ships’ sterns. Meanwhile Ajax sprang on him and pierced his shield, but the spear did not go clean through, though it hustled him back that he could come on no further. He therefore retired a little space from the battlement, yet without losing all his ground, for he still thought to cover himself with glory. Then he turned round and shouted to the brave Lycians saying, “Lycians, why do you thus fail me? For all my prowess I cannot break through the wall and open a way to the ships single-handed. Come close on behind me, for the more there are of us the better.”
units.ja: そこでアイアスとテウクロスの二人が彼を攻めかかった。テウクロスは、彼の体を覆う盾を支える帯に矢を当てたが、ゼウスはわが子を破滅から救い、船尾のもとで倒れさせまいとした。その間にアイアスが彼に飛びかかって盾を突き通したが、槍は完全に貫通はしなかったものの、彼を突き押しやってこれ以上進めなくさせた。それゆえ彼は胸壁から少しばかり後退したが、地歩をすべて失ったわけではなく、まだ自分に名誉を勝ち取ろうと考えていた。そこで彼は振り返り、勇敢なリュキア勢に呼びかけた。「リュキア勢よ、なぜお前たちはこうして私を見捨てるのか。私の武勇をもってしても、一人で城壁を破り、船への道を開くことはできない。私の後ろにぴったりと続け。われらが多ければ多いほどよいのだ。」

notes.title: サルペドンはゼウスの子
notes.body: リュキアの武将サルペドンはゼウスの子であるとされる。ここで「ゼウスはわが子を救った」とあるのはそのためで、神の子の運命と、それでも避けられない死との緊張が物語の背景にある。
notes.titleEn: Sarpedon Is a Son of Zeus
notes.bodyEn: The Lycian commander Sarpedon is said to be a son of Zeus. That is why it says here that "Zeus saved his own son," and the tension between the fate of a god's son and the death that cannot after all be avoided lies in the background of the story.

units.en: The Lycians, shamed by his rebuke, pressed closer round him who was their counsellor and their king. The Argives on their part got their men in fighting order within the wall, and there was a deadly struggle between them. The Lycians could not break through the wall and force their way to the ships, nor could the Danaans drive the Lycians from the wall now that they had once reached it. As two men, measuring-rods in hand, quarrel about their boundaries in a field that they own in common, and stickle for their rights though they be but in a mere strip, even so did the battlements now serve as a bone of contention, and they beat one another’s round shields for their possession. Many a man’s body was wounded with the pitiless bronze, as he turned round and bared his back to the foe, and many were struck clean through their shields; the wall and battlements were everywhere deluged with the blood alike of Trojans and of Achaeans. But even so the Trojans could not rout the Achaeans, who still held on; and as some honest hard-working woman weighs wool in her balance and sees that the scales be true, for she would gain some pitiful earnings for her little ones, even so was the fight balanced evenly between them till the time came when Jove gave the greater glory to Hector son of Priam, who was first to spring towards the wall of the Achaeans. When he had done so, he cried aloud to the Trojans, “Up, Trojans, break the wall of the Argives, and fling fire upon their ships.”
units.ja: リュキア勢は、彼の叱責に恥じ入って、自分たちの助言者であり王である彼の周りにさらに密集した。アルゴス勢のほうは、城壁の内側で兵を戦闘配置につけ、両者の間に死に物狂いの戦いが起こった。リュキア勢は城壁を破って船へとなだれ込むことはできず、ダナオス勢も、リュキア勢がひとたび城壁に取りついた以上、これを城壁から追い払うことはできなかった。二人の男が測量竿を手に、共有する畑の境界をめぐって争い、わずかな一筋の土地であっても自分の権利を主張して譲らない、ちょうどそのように、胸壁はいまや争いの種となり、それを手に入れようと互いの丸い盾を打ち合った。振り返って敵に背をさらすたび、多くの者の体が無情な青銅に傷つけられ、多くの者が盾ごと貫かれた。城壁も胸壁も、トロイア勢とアカイア勢の血とでいたるところ血の海となった。しかしそれでもトロイア勢は、頑として持ちこたえるアカイア勢を撃退できなかった。働き者の正直な女が、天秤で羊毛を量り、さおが釣り合っているかを確かめる、わが子たちのためにわずかな稼ぎを得ようとしてのことである。ちょうどそのように、戦いは両者の間でつり合っていたが、やがてゼウスがより大きな栄光を、プリモスの子ヘクトルに与える時が来た。彼は誰よりも先にアカイア勢の城壁めがけて躍りかかった。そうして彼は大声でトロイア勢に叫んだ。「立て、トロイア勢よ、アルゴス勢の城壁を破り、奴らの船に火を放て。」

notes.title: アカイア勢・アルゴス勢・ダナオス勢
notes.body: 原文では同じギリシア連合軍が「アカイア勢」「アルゴス勢」「ダナオス勢」と複数の呼び名で語られる。これは叙事詩の定型表現による呼び分けで、別々の集団を指すものではない。
notes.bodyEn: In the source text the same Greek allied army is spoken of under multiple names—"Achaeans," "Argives," and "Danaans." This is a differentiation of names arising from the epic's formulaic expressions, and it does not refer to separate groups.

units.en: Thus did he hound them on, and in one body they rushed straight at the wall as he had bidden them, and scaled the battlements with sharp spears in their hands. Hector laid hold of a stone that lay just outside the gates and was thick at one end but pointed at the other; two of the best men in a town, as men now are, could hardly raise it from the ground and put it on to a waggon, but Hector lifted it quite easily by himself, for the son of scheming Saturn made it light for him. As a shepherd picks up a ram’s fleece with one hand and finds it no burden, so easily did Hector lift the great stone and drive it right at the doors that closed the gates so strong and so firmly set. These doors were double and high, and were kept closed by two cross-bars to which there was but one key. When he had got close up to them, Hector strode towards them that his blow might gain in force and struck them in the middle, leaning his whole weight against them. He broke both hinges, and the stone fell inside by reason of its great weight. The portals re-echoed with the sound, the bars held no longer, and the doors flew open, one one way, and the other the other, through the force of the blow. Then brave Hector leaped inside with a face as dark as that of flying night. The gleaming bronze flashed fiercely about his body and he had two spears in his hand. None but a god could have withstood him as he flung himself into the gateway, and his eyes glared like fire. Then he turned round towards the Trojans and called on them to scale the wall, and they did as he bade them—some of them at once climbing over the wall, while others passed through the gates. The Danaans then fled panic-stricken towards their ships, and all was uproar and confusion.
units.ja: こうして彼は彼らを駆り立て、彼らは命じられたとおり、一団となってまっすぐ城壁に殺到し、手に鋭い槍を握って胸壁をよじ登った。ヘクトルは、門のすぐ外にあった石をつかんだ。一端は厚く、他端はとがった石である。今の人間なら、町で最も力のある者二人でも、地面から持ち上げて荷車に載せるのは難しいであろうが、ヘクトルはただ一人でいともたやすく持ち上げた。工謀に長けたサトゥルヌスの子が、彼のためにそれを軽くしたからである。羊飼いが片手で雄羊の毛皮を取り上げ、重荷とも思わない、ちょうどそのように、ヘクトルはその大きな石をたやすく持ち上げ、頑丈に、堅固に据えられた門を閉ざす扉めがけてまっすぐに投げつけた。この扉は二枚合わせの高い扉で、かんぬき二本で閉ざされており、その鍵は一本しかなかった。彼がそれに近づくと、ヘクトルは打撃の勢いを増そうと大股に歩み寄り、全体重をかけて扉の真ん中を打った。彼は蝶番を二つとも壊し、石はその重さゆえに内側へ落ちた。門はその音を響かせ、かんぬきはもはや持ちこたえず、扉は打撃の力で、一方は一方へ、他方は他方へと開き放たれた。そこで勇敢なヘクトルは、飛び去る夜のように暗い顔つきで内側へ躍り込んだ。輝く青銅が彼の体のあたりで激しくきらめき、彼は手に二本の槍を持っていた。彼が門のなかへ突進してくるのを、神ならぬ者に耐えられる者はなかった。その目は炎のように燃えていた。彼は振り返ってトロイア勢に向かい、城壁をよじ登るよう呼びかけると、彼らは命じられたとおりにした。すぐに城壁を乗り越える者もあれば、門を通り抜ける者もあった。ダナオス勢はそのとき恐慌に陥って船へと逃げ、あたりは大混乱となった。

notes.title: 「サトゥルヌスの子」とはゼウス
notes.body: ここで石を軽くした「工謀に長けたサトゥルヌスの子」はゼウスを指す。サトゥルヌスはギリシア神話のクロノスにあたり、その子がゼウスである。ローマ名を用いた呼び方である。
notes.bodyEn: The "son of Saturn, skilled in craft" who here lightened the stone refers to Zeus. Saturn corresponds to Chronos in Greek myth, and his son is Zeus. It is a way of naming him that uses the Roman name.
